title: Best Attack Surface Management Tools in 2026: 12 Compared
summary: Compare 12 attack surface management tools for 2026: how each finds assets, whether it proves what is exploitable, how it is priced and who it fits.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR**


-


The attack surface management market has split into two jobs. Most tools are excellent at **discovery** , finding the assets you forgot you own. Very few do **validation** , proving which of those exposures actually reach critical data.


-


The best choice depends on your gap. For **seedless discovery and shadow IT** , CyCognito leads. For **internet-scale discovery data** , Censys. For **Microsoft or Palo Alto estates** , the matching platform EASM is the easiest economics.


-


For teams that want **impact, not just inventory** ,[CodeAnt AI](https://codeant.ai/) sits in the validation tier. It maps the external surface and then proves which exposures chain through code, cloud, and identity to real data.


-


Gartner folded external attack surface management into its broader[continuous threat exposure management (CTEM)](https://cloudsecurityalliance.org/articles/the-transformative-power-of-continuous-threat-exposure-management-myth-or-reality) framework, where discovery is one stage and validation is the stage that decides what matters.


-


The honest pattern across every tool below: strong on discovery, thin on validation. That gap is the real buying decision.


Your attack surface grows with every deploy. Every new subdomain, container, API, cloud resource, and AI-generated service is another place an attacker can start, and it appears faster than any team can track by hand.


Attack surface management (ASM) software exists to find those exposures before an attacker does. The market is crowded and, on a feature page, most of the tools look the same.


Gartner has been pushing teams past plain discovery for years. It introduced[continuous threat exposure management](https://cloudsecurityalliance.org/articles/the-transformative-power-of-continuous-threat-exposure-management-myth-or-reality) in 2022, predicted that organizations running a CTEM program would be three times less likely to suffer a breach by 2026, and in November 2025 launched its first Magic Quadrant for Exposure Assessment Platforms. In that framework, external attack surface management is one stage, and validation is a separate stage.


That split is the whole story of this guide. Most ASM tools answer "what is exposed." Far fewer answer the question that decides your week, which is "what does this exposure actually reach."


## Who This Guide Is For


This guide is for security leaders, exposure-management owners, and CISOs evaluating attack surface management software in 2026.


If you are asking "which tool finds the most assets" and "which tool tells me which of those assets can actually get me breached," this guide separates the two, because most tools are much better at the first than the second.


If you want the quick version: CyCognito and Censys lead on discovery breadth, the platform EASM tools win on integration economics inside their own ecosystems, and CodeAnt AI is the option for teams that want proven paths from an exposure to critical data rather than another inventory.


## What Does Attack Surface Management Software Do?


Attack surface management (ASM) software finds the systems your organization exposes, keeps that inventory current as things change, and flags the exposures that need fixing. It is the tooling behind two outcomes in the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0: keeping inventories of the hardware, software, services and systems you manage ([ID.AM](http://id.am/) -01 and[ID.AM](http://id.am/) -02), and identifying, validating and recording vulnerabilities in those assets (ID.RA-01).


The terms overlap, so here is how vendors use them in 2026:


Term


What it means


What it covers


ASM


Attack surface management


Discovery and monitoring of exposed assets, internal and external


EASM


External attack surface management


Only what is reachable from the internet: domains, subdomains, IPs, ports, certificates, cloud services, web apps and APIs


CAASM


Cyber asset attack surface management


An internal inventory built by pulling data from the tools you already run (identity, endpoint, cloud, CMDB)


CTEM


Continuous threat exposure management


Gartner's name for the ongoing program that uses these tools: scope, discover, prioritize, validate and fix


Penetration test


A tester or AI agent tries to exploit what is exposed


Proof of what an attacker can actually do, with evidence an auditor or customer accepts


Gartner describes CTEM as a way to continually evaluate how accessible, exposed and exploitable your assets are, and predicted that by 2026 organizations prioritizing security spend through a CTEM program would see a two-thirds reduction in breaches.


The tools in this guide fall into three groups:


-


Discovery-first EASM platforms (CyCognito, Censys, Cortex Xpanse, IONIX) are built to find what you do not know you own.


-


ASM modules inside a larger platform (Microsoft, Google, Rapid7, Tenable, Qualys, CrowdStrike) feed what they find into the vulnerability, threat intelligence or detection tools you already pay for.


-


Tools that pair monitoring with testing go one step further and try to exploit what they find. CyCognito, Cortex Xpanse, Google and IONIX run limited safe checks; CodeAnt AI and Intruder sell full pentests alongside monitoring.


## How We Compared These Tools


We compared each tool on seven questions a security lead asks before buying:


1.


What do you have to give it to start: nothing, a company name, or a list of seeds (domains, IP ranges, ASNs)?


2.


How does it discover assets, and how often does it look again?


3.


Does it test whether an exposure is exploitable, and how safely?


4.


What does it cover: external only, or internal assets too; cloud, web apps, APIs, certificates, third parties?


5.


What do you get back, and where does it go (ticketing, SIEM, SOAR, vulnerability management)?


6.


How is it priced, and is the price public?


7.


What are its documented limits?


Every fact comes from the vendor's own product pages, documentation, pricing pages and, where they rendered, review pages, read in November 2026. We did not run the tools side by side, so where a vendor makes a performance claim we say it is the vendor's claim.

## 1. CodeAnt AI: Best for Impact, Not Just Inventory


**What it is:** external attack surface monitoring combined with AI penetration testing. It is built for security leaders who need to know which exposures an attacker could actually use, and who owe an auditor, a bank partner or an enterprise customer a pentest report.


**How it works:** you give CodeAnt a root domain. It builds the public asset map from what resolves on the internet, using certificate transparency logs, DNS brute-forcing, subdomain takeover checks and port scanning, and keeps monitoring that surface 365 days a year. New subdomains and newly opened ports are picked up as they appear and raised as alerts. On top of the map, AI agents run a black box pentest: they chain exposures into attack paths and try to reach real data. A finding counts only when a working exploit proves it, and security researchers check every critical finding before it reaches you. Grey box adds credentials so the test can try role, tenant and access control abuse; white box adds code and cloud context. The report arrives within 48 hours, with findings mapped to SOC 2 and ISO 27001, and a fixed issue gets a free re-scan.


**What it covers:** monitoring covers everything reachable from the internet. Pentests cover web apps, APIs, cloud, Kubernetes, Active Directory, and internal and external networks.


**Strengths:**


-


It answers "is this exploitable?" with a working exploit, not a severity score.


-


Monitoring and pentest evidence come from one provider, so a new exposure can be tested instead of just listed.


-


A report within 48 hours that an auditor or customer can read.


-


A clear path from black box to grey box to white box as the program matures.


**Proof:** CodeAnt AI has run 12,000 pentests and is trusted by more than 1,000 companies, including Fortune 500 companies like NRG, cybersecurity leaders like Commvault, and fast-growing companies like 11x and Sanas. Its research team has published 100+ CVEs as a VulnCheck CNA partner, including CVE-2026-29000 in pac4j-jwt (CVSS 10.0) and CVE-2026-28292 in simple-git (CVSS 9.8). CodeAnt is SOC 2 Type II and a Gartner Cool Vendor 2026.


**Keep in mind:** monitoring is outside-in only. CodeAnt does not build an internal asset inventory from your identity, endpoint and CMDB tools the way Rapid7 Surface Command or Qualys CSAM do, and it is not an internet-wide research dataset like Censys. It is a managed pentest program, not a self-serve scanner toolbox.


**Pricing and how you buy it:** attack surface monitoring and pentests are quoted together, priced per pentest based on your attack surface.


**Best for:** teams that already know roughly what they own and now need proof of what is exploitable, plus a pentest report, on a regular rhythm.


See your attack surface and what is exploitable in it:[https://codeant.ai/pentesting](https://codeant.ai/pentesting)


## 2. CyCognito: Best for Seedless Discovery and Shadow IT


**What it is:** an external attack surface platform that CyCognito now calls preemptive exposure management, sold as modules for discovery, active exposure validation, exploit intelligence and AI pentesting. It suits large organizations with many subsidiaries, brands or acquisitions.


**How it works:** you give it only your organization's name, with no IP ranges or asset lists. CyCognito builds an organizational graph from DNS analysis, certificate transparency logs, web crawling, port scanning and relationship modeling, then attributes each asset to a subsidiary, brand or business unit with evidence you can review. Discovery refreshes daily, which CyCognito says is the highest frequency available. Its testing module runs payload-based tests directly against each asset using unauthenticated black box techniques, which CyCognito says involve no brute force, no state changes and no disruption to production. It describes 100,000+ attack scenarios across 30+ threat categories, and its AI agents chain exposures across apps, APIs, cloud and AI services.


**What it covers:** externally reachable assets only, including cloud (AWS, Azure, GCP and SaaS), web apps and APIs, subsidiaries and third-party connected systems.


**Strengths:**


-


No seed list: it starts from your company name.


-


Ownership attribution with evidence, down to subsidiary and business unit.


-


Active testing that separates exploitable issues from theoretical ones.


-


Useful during an acquisition, when nobody has a list of what the new company owns.


**Limitations:** it does not see internal assets. Daily is the fastest refresh. Some performance claims, such as reducing pentest time by 70%+, come without a stated method, and the pages do not claim leaked credential monitoring.


**Pricing and how you buy it:** quote only. ASM is priced on total asset volume; the validation and exploit intelligence modules are priced on the number of active IPs and web applications. The quote form asks for an asset bracket (up to 5,000 through 100,001+) and a scan frequency from monthly to daily. There is no trial; CyCognito offers a free risk assessment. G2 shows 4.3 out of 5 from 5 reviews.


**Best for:** large, decentralized organizations that do not know everything they own.


## 3. Palo Alto Cortex Xpanse: Best for Large Palo Alto Estates


**What it is:** Palo Alto's external attack surface product, still sold as Cortex Xpanse (current documentation: Xpanse Expander 2.14, July 2026), for enterprise and government security operations teams. Palo Alto also sells cloud attack surface management inside Cortex Cloud, using Xpanse's outside-in data.


**How it works:** Xpanse scans the entire IPv4 space up to several times a day, maps assets to the people and business units that own them, and raises alerts and incidents with risk scores. Remediation can run automatically through Cortex XSOAR playbooks, and Xpanse Assess gives point-in-time snapshots. With your approval, Attack Surface Testing runs benign exploits against externally facing assets to confirm that a vulnerability is present. Tests run daily based on your preferences, each test is labeled by how intrusive it is, and release 2.14 added an on-demand retest from an alert.


**What it covers:** external assets, including unmanaged cloud assets (with Prisma Cloud), supply chain partners, third-party vendors and acquired companies.


**Strengths:**


-


Very frequent scanning of the whole IPv4 space.


-


Exploit confirmation through Attack Surface Testing.


-


Automated remediation for teams already running XSOAR.


-


Ownership mapping by business unit.


**Limitations:** Palo Alto's documentation says Attack Surface Testing scans are typically not CFAA compliant and may attempt more extensive fuzzing, which is why they run only with approval; plan for legal sign-off. The public pages describe neither seed input nor pricing.


**Pricing and how you buy it:** no price, licensing or edition detail is published; the path is a demo request.


**Best for:** large enterprises already invested in Palo Alto's Cortex stack.


## 4. Microsoft Defender EASM: Best for Microsoft and Azure Teams


**What it is:** an Azure resource that continuously discovers and maps your digital attack surface, for security and IT teams that run on Microsoft.


**How it works:** you add seeds (domains, IP blocks, hosts, email contacts, ASNs or Whois organizations) or import a prebuilt inventory for your organization. Defender EASM runs recursive searches through Whois, DNS, SSL certificate and ASN records and labels each asset Confirmed, Candidate or Requires Investigation. It scans assets with Microsoft's virtual user technology, and discovery groups can be scheduled to run on a recurring basis. Attack Surface Insights dashboards summarize vulnerabilities, compliance and security hygiene.


It also connects to the rest of Microsoft security. Defender CSPM includes the EASM integration by default without a separate Defender EASM licence, and Microsoft Security Exposure Management offers a prebuilt external footprint without a full subscription; full integration needs a Defender EASM subscription.


**What it covers:** external domains, IPs, hosts, ASNs, web applications, third-party dependencies and SSL certificates.


**Strengths:**


-


Billed on your Azure invoice, with a 30-day free trial.


-


Recursive discovery with clear confidence labels.


-


Feeds Defender for Cloud and Exposure Management.


**Limitations:** seeds are required, there is no exploit validation, and Microsoft does not publish a rescan interval. In Exposure Management, external attack surface assets do not support scoping, so everyone with access sees all of the collected data.


**Pricing and how you buy it:** after the 30-day trial you are charged automatically per billable asset, counted as approved host and IP pairs, IPs and domains seen within the last 30 days, on your Azure bill. Check the current rate on Microsoft's pricing page. As of November 2026, Microsoft's Defender EASM documentation shows no retirement notice. G2 shows 4.3 out of 5 from 17 reviews.


**Best for:** Microsoft-centric organizations that want external discovery inside the tools they already use.


## 5. Censys ASM: Best for Discovery Accuracy


**What it is:** Censys Attack Surface Management, part of the Censys Platform and built on the Censys Internet Map, the company's own internet-wide scan data. It is aimed at exposure management teams.


**How it works:** you add seeds (domains, IPs or CIDR blocks, and ASNs) through the console, a CSV upload or the API, and can connect cloud accounts so cloud assets and storage buckets seed themselves. Censys attributes assets through DNS and certificates, maps exposure across all 65,535 ports with first-party scanning, and ranks risks by severity, category and affected asset. Web assets come with technologies, JavaScript libraries, screenshots and redirect chains, and there are trend views and executive reports.


**What it covers:** external assets, certificates (including self-signed certificates and reissue alerts), web properties and cloud assets through connectors.


**Strengths:**


-


Its own scanning across every port, not a resold dataset.


-


Strong certificate and dangling DNS visibility.


-


Cloud connectors that keep cloud seeds current.


-


Clear risk ranking by severity and asset.


**Limitations:** you have to supply seeds. Censys's documentation says certificates are never used as seeds, a certificate is not used for discovery if your organization does not own every name on it, some relationships rely on records from the past 270 days, and wrongly attributed assets must be excluded manually. Censys does not describe exploit validation; its advisories help you confirm whether an asset is reachable.


**Pricing and how you buy it:** contact sales. ASM is listed separately from the Core, Adversary Investigation and Security Operations plans, none of which show a price. A free Censys account covers search, not ASM. G2 shows 4.8 out of 5 from 3 reviews.


**Best for:** teams that want the most detailed internet-facing data and have the people to tune seeds and attribution.


## 6. CrowdStrike Falcon Surface: Best for CrowdStrike Customers


Falcon Surface is CrowdStrike's external attack surface module, and like most things in the CrowdStrike world it is designed to pull another security function into the Falcon platform rather than stand on its own. CrowdStrike earned its reputation in endpoint detection and threat intelligence, and Falcon Surface extends that same lens outward to internet-facing assets. For the large base of organizations that already treat Falcon as their security backbone, the appeal is consolidation rather than novelty. It is rarely the tool a team adopts in isolation from the rest of the platform.


**Best for:** existing CrowdStrike customers consolidating within one platform.


**How it works:** continuous external discovery and real-time monitoring feed risk scoring into the Falcon console, enriched with CrowdStrike threat intelligence.


**Strengths:**


-


Consolidates external exposure into a console teams already use every day.


-


Continuous monitoring with CrowdStrike threat context.


-


Fast to adopt for existing Falcon customers.


**Limitation:** the economics favor existing Falcon customers, and it scores risk rather than proving an end-to-end path.


**Pricing:** custom, as part of the Falcon platform. Contact sales for a quote.


## 7. Tenable One ASM: Best for Tenable Customers


Tenable is one of the longest-standing names in vulnerability management, the company behind Nessus, and its ASM capability is part of a deliberate shift from vulnerability management toward broader exposure management under the Tenable One banner. For an installed base that has run Tenable for years, external discovery is a natural extension of a familiar workflow. The story it tells is less about novel discovery and more about keeping every exposure in one platform. That continuity is the main reason existing customers choose it over a standalone EASM tool.


**Best for:** teams already invested in Tenable for vulnerability management.


**How it works:** external discovery feeds the Tenable One exposure platform, landing external findings alongside internal vulnerability data under one scoring model.


**Strengths:**


-


Workflow continuity with Tenable vulnerability management.


-


Part of a broader exposure-management platform.


-


Familiar scoring and reporting for existing customers.


**Limitation:** validation stays at the level of vulnerability correlation rather than proven attack paths.


**Pricing:** custom, as part of Tenable One. Contact sales for a quote.


## 8. Qualys EASM: Best for Qualys Customers


Qualys is another vulnerability-management veteran, known for delivering its scanning entirely from the cloud and for its VMDR product, and its EASM capability follows the same logic as Tenable's. The company's enduring strength has been breadth of scanning from a single cloud platform. Adding external discovery lets it offer a one-console story to the enterprises that already depend on it. As with Tenable, its pull is integration and familiarity rather than leadership in discovery itself.


**Best for:** teams already running Qualys for vulnerability management.


**How it works:** agentless external discovery surfaces unknown internet-facing assets and feeds them into Qualys VMDR, so exposures flow through existing workflows.


**Strengths:**


-


Single console shared with Qualys VMDR.


-


Agentless discovery of unknown assets.


-


Continuity with established Qualys processes.


**Limitation:** like Tenable, validation is correlation with vulnerability data rather than path proof.


**Pricing:** custom, as part of the Qualys platform. Contact sales for a quote.


## 9. Mandiant ASM: Best for Adversary-Aware Prioritization


Mandiant is one of the most respected incident-response and threat-intelligence firms in the industry, the team called in after many of the decade's largest breaches, and it is now part of Google Cloud. Its attack surface product is distinctive because it is backed by that frontline intelligence rather than by discovery technology alone. Where most tools rank exposures by generic severity, Mandiant can weight them by what its responders are watching attackers actually do. That intelligence pedigree, more than its scanning, is what sets it apart.


**Best for:** teams that want threat-intelligence-aware prioritization.


**How it works:** continuous discovery is paired with Mandiant frontline threat intelligence, now part of Google Cloud, ranking exposures by adversary activity and running active checks on discovered assets.


**Strengths:**


-


Prioritization informed by Mandiant threat intelligence.


-


Active checks on discovered exposures.


-


Adversary context that most pure-discovery tools lack.


**Limitation:** the threat context sharpens ranking, but it still stops short of proving an end-to-end path through your environment.


**Pricing:** custom, via Google Cloud. Contact sales for a quote.


## 10. IONIX: Best for Mapping Connected Third-Party Risk


IONIX, formerly Cyberpion, built its approach around a specific observation: your real attack surface includes everything your assets connect to, not only the assets you own. That means third-party scripts, cloud dependencies, and the long chain of services a single application quietly relies on. It is a narrower and more opinionated take on ASM than the broad-discovery platforms around it. The teams drawn to it usually run dependency-heavy or deeply interconnected environments where that connective risk is the thing that actually keeps them up at night.


**Best for:** teams whose risk lives in dependencies and connected third-party assets.


**How it works:** IONIX maps not only your assets but the third-party and dependency relationships that extend the surface, then runs targeted exploit testing on discovered exposures.


**Strengths:**


-


Maps the connective tissue and third-party dependencies, not just owned assets.


-


Active exploit testing on discovered exposures.


-


Focused prioritization of the connections that extend your risk.


**Limitation:** an external platform, so it does not reach into internal code and identity context.


**Pricing:** custom. Contact sales for a quote.


## 11. Intruder: Best for Lean Teams


**What it is:** always-on exposure management for lean security teams, combining attack surface monitoring, vulnerability scanning, cloud security, DAST and, since July 2026, an AI pentest.


**How it works:** you connect AWS, Azure or Google Cloud accounts (synced every two hours) or add IPs and domains. Subdomain discovery uses DNS reconnaissance and passive DNS, daily on Enterprise and weekly on Cloud and Pro, and Intruder does not add discovered subdomains to scanning automatically. Emerging threat scans start by themselves when a new critical issue is published, against your active external targets. Scanning covers 140,000+ checks, with a ZAP-powered DAST scanner that supports authenticated scans.


**What it covers:** external infrastructure, cloud, web apps and APIs; internal targets on Pro and Enterprise.


**Strengths:**


-


Public plans, a free tier and a fast self-serve setup.


-


Cloud sync every two hours catches new cloud assets quickly.


-


Automatic scans when a new critical vulnerability appears.


**Limitations:** automated discovery of unknown assets (shadow IT) is Enterprise only. Port coverage depends on the plan: ports 80 and 443 on Free, the top 10 on Cloud, the top 50 on Pro and all ports on Enterprise. Emerging threat scan results do not update after later scans, and they use licences.


**Pricing and how you buy it:** a Free plan (5 web apps, 3 users, 1 cloud account); Cloud and Pro plans priced as a base fee plus a small fee per target, billed monthly or annually (annual saves 20%); Enterprise by quote; a 14-day trial. The AI pentest costs $3,500 per same-day test or $12,000 for four. G2 shows 4.8 out of 5 from 223 reviews.


**Best for:** small teams that want a price they can see today and can live without automated unknown-asset discovery on the lower plans.


## 12. Rapid7 Surface Command


**What it is:** the attack surface management base of the Rapid7 Command Platform (launched August 2024), combining external discovery (EASM) with an internal asset inventory (CAASM).


**How it works:** you add seeds (registered domains and public IP networks) by hand or through dynamic seed queries from Markmonitor, NetBox or InsightAppSec. Rapid7's External Asset Engine starts scanning seeds immediately and finds subdomains, network services, TLS certificates, IPs and autonomous system data. Connectors pull data from internal tools such as Entra ID, Microsoft Defender and CrowdStrike, typically daily, and an orchestrator reaches on-premises sources such as Active Directory. You get a correlated inventory and asset graph, blast radius analysis and approve or reject decisions on ownership. CISA KEV, EPSS, MITRE ATT&CK and NVD enrichment come pre-installed. Dynamic EASM discovery reached general availability in January 2026.


**What it covers:** internal assets through connectors and external assets through scanning, including certificates. Cloud security, application security and attack path analysis sit in the higher Exposure Command tiers.


**Strengths:**


-


One correlated view of internal and external assets.


-


Vendor-agnostic connectors, so it works alongside other security tools.


-


Dynamic seeds that update from domain registrar and IP management data.


-


An upgrade path into Rapid7 vulnerability management without re-licensing.


**Limitations:** Rapid7's documentation says external discovery depends on the seeds you supply, and on-premises sources need an orchestrator. Surface Command does not validate exposures; Rapid7 shows red team findings only with a separate continuous red teaming licence (Vector Command).


**Pricing and how you buy it:** not public. Rapid7 says pricing reflects the asset types and use cases in scope and tracks billable assets. The product page offers a trial. Rapid7 has no G2 listing for Surface Command.


**Best for:** teams that want one inventory across their IT tools and the internet, especially those already on Rapid7.


## Open-Source Attack Surface Management


If budget is the constraint and you have the in-house skill to operate it, open-source tooling covers the discovery basics.[OWASP Amass](https://owasp.org/www-project-amass/) is the most established, mapping external assets and infrastructure through passive and active reconnaissance.


The trade-off is real. Open-source tools give you discovery and nothing downstream. There is no prioritization engine, no validation, and no managed support, so the operating cost moves from a license to your team's time.


## Do you need attack surface management and a pentest?


Most teams need both, because they answer different questions. Attack surface management answers "what do we expose, and what changed since yesterday?" A penetration test answers "what can an attacker do with it?"


The case for monitoring comes up again and again with security leads. Early infrastructure was often set up by people who have since left, so nobody has a full list of what is public. Teams harden the core product but not the forgotten staging server, the old marketing site or the SDK someone published to a public package registry, and that infrastructure is where attackers start. A scan that runs once a year cannot catch a subdomain created last week.


The case for testing comes up just as often. Discovery tools return what passive data can show: open ports, headers, certificate problems and software versions with known CVEs. They rarely tell you whether an old plugin is actually reachable without authentication, or that a product's default setting lets anyone sign up and log in to your environment. Someone has to try. Dynamic application security testing (DAST) sits in between: it checks one route at a time but does not chain several weaknesses into a path to your data, which is what a pentest does.


A pattern that works for many teams:


1.


Monitor the external attack surface continuously, with alerts for new subdomains, newly opened ports and newly published critical vulnerabilities on software you run.


2.


Pentest on a fixed rhythm (quarterly is common) and after major releases, acquisitions or a spike in probing.


3.


Retest every fix, so the next report shows closed issues, not just open ones.


## How Much Does Attack Surface Management Cost?


Very few vendors publish a price. Of the 12 tools here, only Intruder lists plans on its own site, and even there the Cloud and Pro prices depend on how many targets you scan. Everyone else quotes. What you can compare is the pricing unit, because it decides how the bill grows:

OWASP Amass is free and open source, but you run it, store the results and do the triage yourself.

## Attack Surface Management vs Vulnerability Management vs CTEM


Three terms get used as if they were the same program. They are not, and the difference decides what each tool is for.


Discipline


Core question


What it produces


Vulnerability management


What is wrong with the assets we know about?


A ranked list of CVEs on known assets


Attack surface management


What is exposed, including assets we forgot?


A discovered, monitored inventory of exposures


Attack path analysis and validation


Which exposures actually reach critical data?


Proven routes, prioritized by impact


CTEM (the Gartner program)


How do we run all of the above continuously?


A repeating cycle of scope, discover, prioritize, validate, mobilize


Vulnerability management works on assets you already know. ASM finds the ones you do not. Validation proves which of them matter. CTEM is the program that keeps the loop running, and it is why[prioritization beyond CVSS alone](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog) has become the standard expectation.


The full breakdown of where inventory stops and impact begins is in[attack surface management vs. attack path analysis](https://codeant.ai/blogs/attack-surface-management-vs-attack-path-analysis) .


## What Security Teams Push Back On


"Our ASM tool only gives us headers, known CVEs and configuration checks." That is what passive discovery can see. Ask each vendor whether it tests exploitability, how (benign checks, payload tests or a full pentest), and whether testing needs extra approval. Issues such as an open self-signup setting or an old component reachable without login only show up when something actually tries them.


"We already pay for an outside-in security rating." Ratings services score you for customers and insurers from public data. They do not attack you, so they cannot tell you which exposure leads to your data. Treat a rating as a signal and ASM plus testing as the work.


"Per-asset pricing punishes us for growing." Ask how assets are counted and whether newly discovered assets start billing automatically. Microsoft counts host and IP pairs, IPs and domains seen in the last 30 days; IONIX counts domain names; Intruder keeps a licence in use for 30 days. A vendor that prices on attack surface but adds new subdomains to scope as they appear removes the incentive to leave assets out.


"We pay per pentest, so we cannot test every month." Use monitoring between tests to watch for change, and trigger a test when something material changes: a new app, an acquisition, a burst of probing, or a critical vulnerability in software you expose.


"Will a scan disrupt production?" Every vendor that runs active checks says they are safe, but the details differ: CyCognito says its tests make no state changes, Google keeps scans light and asks you to allowlist its IPs, and Palo Alto runs Attack Surface Testing only with your approval and labels each test by intrusiveness. Ask for the vendor's rules of engagement in writing.


The right attack surface management tool is the one that closes your specific gap: finding what you own, fitting the tools you run, or proving what is exploitable.


## The Bottom Line


The ASM market is full of capable discovery tools, and the right platform EASM is often the one that fits the stack you already run. That solves the first half of the problem, which is knowing what is exposed.


The second half is knowing what those exposures reach. A growing inventory of unranked assets is not the same as a short list of routes to your data, and Gartner's move to fold ASM into a validation-centric CTEM program is a signal that discovery alone is no longer enough. A tool that maps the surface and validates the paths behind it turns that inventory into decisions. That is the layer[CodeAnt AI](https://codeant.ai/) adds on top of discovery.
